messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 66

# The Weight of the Room

Marcus is a 45-year-old investigative journalist who has spent the better part of two decades covering conflict zones across the Middle East and Eastern Europe. His colleagues describe him as meticulous and fearless — a man who believed that bearing witness was the most important work a person could do. That belief was tested, and ultimately fractured, three years ago when he was taken captive while reporting near the Syrian-Turkish border.

He was held for eleven days. In the telling of it, he is precise about the number — eleven days — as though the exactness of that figure is the one thing he can still control. He was kept in a windowless room, bound for much of the time, uncertain whether his captors intended to ransom him, execute him, or simply forget about him. He heard other men being beaten in adjacent rooms. He was not given consistent food or water. On the fourth day, he was made to kneel in front of a camera, and he became convinced, with absolute certainty, that he was about to die. He did not die. He was released through a negotiated exchange that he was not informed of until the moment it happened. He walked out into blinding afternoon light and felt, he says, nothing at all.

That numbness lasted about six weeks. Then the room came back.

Marcus now lives in Brussels with his wife, Elise, and their two teenage children. From the outside, he has resumed something resembling his former life. He still works as a journalist, though he has moved to an editorial role and no longer travels to conflict zones — a decision he frames as a professional choice rather than a personal one, though he acknowledges, reluctantly, that he cannot board a plane without his heart hammering against his ribs. He sits with his back to walls in restaurants. He checks the locks on the doors of his house two, sometimes three times before bed, and then lies awake anyway, listening to the house settle around him.

Sleep, when it comes, is rarely safe. He dreams of the room — not always the actual room, but rooms that share its logic: low ceilings, no exits, the sound of footsteps approaching. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, drenched in sweat, briefly unable to remember where he is. Elise has learned not to touch him in those first moments of waking. Early in the first year, she reached for him instinctively, and he grabbed her wrist hard enough to leave a bruise. He still carries the shame of that.

At work, he functions adequately, though his concentration has become unreliable in ways that frustrate him deeply. He was once known for his ability to hold vast amounts of information in his head, to construct complex narratives from scattered details. Now he loses threads mid-sentence. He rereads paragraphs and finds they have left no impression. When a younger colleague recently returned from reporting in Ukraine and described a detention facility he had briefly been held in — speaking about it with the casual bravado Marcus once recognized in himself — Marcus stood up from the editorial meeting and left the room without explanation. He sat in the bathroom for twenty minutes, breathing carefully, waiting for his hands to stop shaking.

He does not talk about what happened with Elise, not really. She knows the outline. She does not know that he still, three years later, wakes some mornings and spends several seconds genuinely uncertain whether the life around him is real or whether the room is the truth and everything else is the dream. He has started to suspect that the person who walked out into that afternoon light was not quite the same person who had walked in — and that the distance between those two men may be permanent.

He is not sure what to do with that suspicion. So mostly, he says nothing.
